stem: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, delivers a healthy newborn at 39 weeks of gestation. Her blood type is O Rh(D)-negative, and antibody screens at her initial prenatal visit and at 28 weeks were negative. She received 300 micrograms of Rh(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks. Delivery is uncomplicated, with an estimated blood loss of 350 mL. Cord blood testing shows that the newborn is Rh(D)-positive. A postpartum maternal rosette test for significant fetomaternal hemorrhage is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate management to prevent Rh alloimmunization?
A: Withhold postpartum Rh(D) immune globulin because the rosette test is negative
B: Administer 50 micrograms of Rh(D) immune globulin to the mother within 72 hours of delivery
C: Administer 300 micrograms of Rh(D) immune globulin to the mother within 72 hours of delivery
D: Defer Rh(D) immune globulin until the 6-week postpartum visit
E: Administer Rh(D) immune globulin only if maternal anti-D antibodies become detectable

stem: A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus uses insulin lispro before meals and insulin glargine nightly. He is preparing for an examination and asks when he should inject each medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate timing for these insulins?
A: Lispro immediately before eating and glargine once daily at the same time each day
B: Lispro 30–60 minutes before eating and glargine immediately after meals
C: Lispro at bedtime and glargine immediately before each meal
D: Lispro once daily in the morning and glargine 30 minutes before each meal
E: Lispro 2 hours after eating and glargine only when fasting blood glucose is elevated

stem: A 52-year-old woman has bothersome hot flashes and night sweats that disrupt sleep. Her last menstrual period was 14 months ago. She has an intact uterus and no history of venous thromboembolism, breast cancer, coronary artery disease, or liver disease. She wants the most effective treatment for her symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
A: Oral conjugated estrogen alone
D: Paroxetine therapy

stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of abdominal pain for 14 hours. The pain began around the umbilicus and is now localized to the right lower quadrant. She has had nausea and two episodes of vomiting and has no appetite. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 98/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows tenderness and voluntary guarding at the right lower quadrant; palpation of the left lower quadrant elicits pain in the right lower quadrant. Pelvic examination shows no cervical motion tenderness or discharge. Leukocyte count is 14,800/mm3 with 82% neutrophils. A urine pregnancy test is negative, and urinalysis shows 2 leukocytes/hpf and no nitrites. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Abdominal radiography
B: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast
D: Barium enema

stem: A previously healthy 3-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because of a 2-day history of fever, irritability, and refusal to eat. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). Examination shows several shallow ulcers on the tongue and buccal mucosa as well as scattered 2- to 3-mm vesicles on the palms and soles. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Intravenous acyclovir
D: Topical triamcinolone

stem: A 68-year-old woman comes to the office because of difficulty sleeping for the past 8 months. She reports that it takes her more than an hour to fall asleep and that she awakens two or three times nightly, often lying awake worrying about whether she will be able to function the next day. She goes to bed at 8:30 PM to "get enough rest" and stays in bed until 8:00 AM, frequently napping for 1-2 hours in the afternoon. She drinks one cup of coffee in the morning and no alcohol. She has hypertension controlled with amlodipine and osteoarthritis of the knees that does not wake her at night. She denies snoring, restless legs, depressed mood, or anhedonia; her husband confirms she does not snore or kick during sleep. Physical examination and laboratory studies, including thyroid function tests, are unremarkable. Her score on a depression screening instrument is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia
D: Low-dose quetiapine at bedtime

stem: A 64-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 40-pack-year smoking history presents to the emergency department with 45 minutes of crushing substernal chest pressure radiating to his left arm. He is diaphoretic and nauseated. Blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg, pulse is 88/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. ECG shows 2-mm ST-segment elevations in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST depressions in leads I and aVL. He has no history of gastrointestinal bleeding, stroke, or anticoagulant use. The nearest percutaneous coronary intervention-capable hospital is 20 minutes away. After administration of aspirin, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Administer sublingual nitroglycerin and observe for resolution of symptoms
C: Activate the cardiac catheterization laboratory for primary percutaneous coronary intervention
D: Obtain serial cardiac troponin measurements before deciding on reperfusion therapy
E: Administer supplemental oxygen by nonrebreather mask

stem: A 52-year-old woman undergoes core-needle biopsy of a 1.8-cm palpable mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, which shows invasive ductal carcinoma. Mammography and breast MRI show a solitary lesion without chest wall involvement, and there is no clinical evidence of axillary lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. She has no pathogenic BRCA mutation, no prior breast irradiation, and wishes to preserve her breast. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial surgical management?
A: Breast-conserving surgery with sentinel lymph node biopsy followed by adjuvant whole-breast radiation
C: Modified radical mastectomy with complete axillary lymph node dissection
D: Breast-conserving surgery without axillary staging followed by endocrine therapy alone
E: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by mastectomy regardless of treatment response

stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after his motorcycle struck a guardrail. He was wearing a helmet and did not lose consciousness. He complains of left-sided chest and upper abdominal pain. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg. He is alert and oriented. Examination shows tenderness over the left lower ribs and the left upper quadrant with mild guarding; the pelvis is stable and there are no long-bone deformities. Two liters of warmed crystalloid are infused, after which his pulse is 92/min and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Hemoglobin concentration is 11.2 g/dL. Focused assessment with sonography for trauma demonstrates free fluid in the left upper quadrant and pelvis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen shows a 5-cm laceration of the spleen with a 2-cm area of contrast extravasation within the splenic parenchyma and moderate hemoperitoneum; no other injuries are identified. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Immediate exploratory laparotomy with splenectomy
D: Admission for observation with serial hematocrit measurements and bed rest alone

stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with a 1-week history of a painful, erythematous, and edematous right lower extremity that has progressively worsened despite over-the-counter analgesics. On examination, the area is warm to touch, tender, and there is a 2 cm ulcer on the medial malleolus with purulent drainage. Laboratory studies reveal an elevated white blood cell count with a left shift and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/h. A tissue biopsy of the ulcer edge shows numerous neutrophils and vascular congestion. Which of the following best characterizes the type of inflammation present in this patient?
A: Acute inflammation, characterized by neutrophil predominance and vascular changes
B: Chronic inflammation, characterized by lymphocytic infiltration and fibrosis
C: Granulomatous inflammation, characterized by multinucleated giant cells and caseous necrosis
D: Serous inflammation, characterized by a clear fluid exudate
E: Fibrinous inflammation, characterized by a fibrin-rich exudate forming a meshwork

stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with 2 days of fever, sore throat, and painful swallowing. He has no cough or rhinorrhea. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F). Examination shows tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical lymph nodes, and no splenomegaly. A rapid antigen detection test for group A Streptococcus is positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
A: Amoxicillin for 10 days
D: Clindamycin for 10 days
E: Penicillin G benzathine as a single intramuscular dose

stem: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, at 39 weeks' gestation is in active labor. She has received oxytocin for 4 hours with an intrauterine pressure catheter documenting 220 Montevideo units. Cervical examination remains unchanged at 7 cm dilation, 90% effacement, and 0 station. The fetal heart rate pattern is category I. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Administer terbutaline
D: Perform forceps-assisted vaginal delivery

stem: A 27-year-old woman at 37 weeks' gestation presents for a routine prenatal visit. Her rectovaginal culture obtained at 36 weeks is positive for group B Streptococcus. She reports that as a teenager she developed generalized urticaria, lip swelling, and wheezing within 30 minutes of taking amoxicillin, requiring treatment in an emergency department. She has no other medical problems and takes only a prenatal vitamin. Susceptibility testing on the group B Streptococcus isolate reveals resistance to clindamycin and erythromycin. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent for intrapartum prophylaxis?
A: Cefazolin
B: Penicillin G after rapid oral desensitization
D: Clindamycin

stem: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 18 hours of abdominal pain that began near the umbilicus and migrated to the right lower quadrant. He has nausea and anorexia but no diarrhea or urinary symptoms. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg, and pulse is 96/min. Abdominal examination shows focal tenderness and guarding at McBurney point with pain on percussion. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 14,200/mm3 with neutrophilia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?
A: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
D: Plain abdominal radiography

stem: A 22-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department 2 hours after a head injury during a football game. He was tackled and hit his head on the ground, but did not lose consciousness. He reports headache, dizziness, and mild confusion. He has no focal neurologic deficits. A noncontrast head CT is normal. He is diagnosed with a concussion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Advise relative cognitive and physical rest for 24 to 48 hours, then gradual return to activities as tolerated
B: Discharge home with instructions to avoid all physical activity for 2 weeks
C: Discharge home with instructions to avoid all cognitive activity for 1 week
D: Prescribe acetaminophen with codeine for headache and discharge home
E: Recommend strict bed rest until all symptoms have resolved

stem: A 2-day-old term newborn is evaluated for yellow discoloration of the skin. He was delivered vaginally after an uncomplicated pregnancy. He is breastfeeding every 2 to 3 hours and has had 3 wet diapers and 2 stools in the past 24 hours. Physical examination shows jaundice of the face and upper chest without hepatosplenomegaly or bruising. Total serum bilirubin is 9 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin is 0.3 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Begin intensive phototherapy
D: Obtain a direct antiglobulin test
E: Repeat total serum bilirubin measurement within 24 hours

stem: A 7-month-old boy is brought for poor weight gain. He was born at term with a normal birth weight and has been exclusively breastfed. His weight has fallen from the 50th percentile at birth to below the 5th percentile, while length and head circumference remain at the 25th percentile. He feeds for 5 minutes every 3-4 hours and often falls asleep at the breast. He has 5-6 wet diapers daily and no vomiting, diarrhea, recurrent infections, sweating with feeds, or respiratory symptoms. Development is age-appropriate. Physical examination is normal except for decreased subcutaneous fat; there are no murmurs, hepatomegaly, or dysmorphic features. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Hospitalize for comprehensive laboratory evaluation, including metabolic studies
B: Obtain an echocardiogram to evaluate for congenital heart disease
C: Observe a breastfeeding session and provide feeding counseling with close weight follow-up
D: Order stool studies for malabsorption, including fecal elastase and reducing substances
E: Start empiric proton pump inhibitor therapy for gastroesophageal reflux

stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe pain in his left forearm 6 hours after sustaining a closed fracture of the distal radius and ulna following a motor vehicle collision. On examination, the forearm is swollen, tense, and exquisitely tender to palpation. Passive extension of the fingers elicits intense pain, and the radial pulse is weak but palpable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Emergent fasciotomy of the forearm compartments
B: Application of a splint and elevation of the limb
C: Administration of intravenous opioids for pain control
D: Obtaining an urgent MRI to evaluate for soft tissue injury
E: Scheduling urgent orthopedic consultation for external fixation

stem: A 64-year-old man undergoes an uncomplicated laparoscopic-assisted sigmoid colectomy for diverticulitis. On the morning of postoperative day 3, his temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F). He has an indwelling urinary catheter. Examination of the abdomen shows a well-healing incision without erythema or drainage. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's fever?
A: Atelectasis
D: Surgical-site infection

stem: A 45-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with acute pancreatitis due to gallstones. His initial laboratory results show a white blood cell count of 12,000 cells/μL, hematocrit of 42%, and serum creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL. After 48 hours, his condition worsens with increasing abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. His current vital signs are temperature 38.5°C, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, heart rate 120 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Administer intravenous fluids and start antibiotics
C: Order a CT scan of the abdomen with contrast
D: Insert a nasogastric tube for decompression
E: Transfer to the intensive care unit

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding for 6 months. Her cycles are regular every 28 days, but she soaks through a pad or tampon every hour. She has no pelvic pain or dyspareunia. Vital signs are normal. BMI is 32 kg/m². Pelvic exam reveals a symmetrically enlarged uterus, approximately 12 weeks size, with no adnexal masses. A saline infusion sonohysterogram shows a single 3-cm submucosal fibroid. Endometrial biopsy shows proliferative endometrium without hyperplasia or malignancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device
B: Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
D: Oral medroxyprogesterone acetate

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of fatigue, paresthesias in the hands and feet, and a sore tongue. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. His hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is 110 fL, and serum vitamin B12 level is 150 pg/mL (normal range 200-900 pg/mL). Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of his vitamin B12 deficiency?
A: Autoimmune gastritis leading to intrinsic factor deficiency
D: Inadequate dietary intake of vitamin B12

stem: A 66-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of fatigue, night sweats, and abdominal fullness. Physical examination shows nontender cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy and a spleen palpable 6 cm below the left costal margin. Colonoscopy performed for intermittent hematochezia shows numerous small polyps throughout the colon. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 18,000/mm3 with 40% small lymphocytes. Biopsy of a cervical lymph node shows effacement of the normal architecture by a diffuse infiltrate of small to medium-sized lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours. Immunohistochemical staining is positive for CD5, CD20, and cyclin D1 and negative for CD10 and CD23. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A: Burkitt lymphoma
D: Mantle cell lymphoma

stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents for a routine follow-up visit. He has no history of cardiovascular disease. His medications include metformin and lisinopril. Blood pressure is 132/78 mmHg. Fasting lipid panel shows total cholesterol 210 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 135 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol 42 mg/dL, and triglycerides 165 mg/dL. He is started on atorvastatin 40 mg daily. Which of the following is the most appropriate method to monitor this patient's response to therapy?
A: Coronary artery calcium score in 6 months
D: Serum creatine kinase level in 4-12 weeks

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive numbness and tingling in his feet, followed by similar symptoms in his hands. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. On examination, he has decreased vibration sense and proprioception in his distal extremities, with absent ankle reflexes. Which of the following tests is most likely to provide a diagnosis?
A: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography
D: Vitamin B12 level

stem: A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia is brought to the emergency department by his family due to confusion and fever. He was recently discharged from an inpatient psychiatric unit after a medication change. On examination, he is diaphoretic, tachycardic, and has severe generalized muscle rigidity. Temperature is 40.6 C (105.1 F), blood pressure is 168/104 mm Hg, pulse is 122/min, and respirations are 24/min. Laboratory studies show leukocytosis and a markedly elevated creatine kinase level. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Administer dantrolene and bromocriptine
D: Administer cyproheptadine

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought for follow-up 4 weeks after starting methylphenidate for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. His teacher and parents report marked improvement in classroom behavior and task completion. He has no insomnia, headaches, or mood changes. His weight has decreased from 24.0 kg to 23.7 kg, and his height percentile is unchanged. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Continue the current methylphenidate dose with monitoring of growth and adverse effects
C: Discontinue methylphenidate and refer for behavioral therapy alone
D: Increase the methylphenidate dose to improve academic performance
E: Switch from methylphenidate to extended-release guanfacine

stem: A 15-month-old child is brought to the pediatrician for a well-child visit. According to the parents, the child can walk independently, say 'mama' and 'dada' with meaning, and points to objects when asked. The child also follows simple commands like 'give me the ball.' Which of the following developmental milestones is this child most likely delayed in achieving?
A: Building a tower of two blocks
D: Stacking four cubes

stem: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of runny nose, cough, and difficulty breathing. The infant is febrile to 38.5°C (101.3°F), has a respiratory rate of 60 breaths per minute, and is using accessory muscles to breathe. Oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. The diagnosis is bronchiolitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
A: Administer supplemental oxygen to maintain oxygen saturation above 90%
B: Prescribe a course of oral corticosteroids
D: Administer intravenous antibiotics
E: Order a chest radiograph to confirm the diagnosis

stem: A 27-year-old man develops progressive leg weakness and tingling 10 days after an episode of diarrhea. Examination shows symmetric ascending weakness, reduced deep-tendon reflexes, and mild facial weakness. Vital capacity is 18 mL/kg, and arterial blood gas analysis shows a PaCO₂ of 48 mm Hg. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals elevated protein concentration with 2 white blood cells/mm³. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Transfer to the intensive care unit for close respiratory monitoring
D: Obtain magnetic resonance imaging of the spinal cord

stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his roommate, who found him writing a detailed plan to jump off a bridge. The patient has a history of major depressive disorder and has been off his antidepressant medication for 3 weeks due to perceived side effects. On examination, he appears withdrawn, has poor eye contact, and speaks in a low monotone. When asked about his current thoughts, he states, 'I have it all planned out. I have my ticket and I know exactly where to go. I just need to wait for the weekend.' He denies any current intent to act immediately but admits he feels trapped and sees no other way out. His roommate reports that the patient gave away his prized guitar collection yesterday. Which of the following factors in this patient's presentation is most strongly associated with an increased risk of completed suicide?
A: Presence of a detailed suicide plan
D: Recent discontinuation of antidepressant medication

stem: An 11-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of intermittent crying for 8 hours. Episodes last 2 to 3 minutes, during which he draws his legs up and becomes pale; between episodes he is quiet and sleepy. He has vomited twice and passed one stool containing mucus and blood. He had a mild upper respiratory tract infection last week. His temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 148/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg. He appears lethargic but is well perfused. Abdominal examination shows a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant; there is no guarding or distention. Rectal examination shows blood-streaked mucus on the glove. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
A: Abdominal ultrasonography
B: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen
D: Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan
E: Upper gastrointestinal series with small-bowel follow-through

stem: A 16-year-old boy is evaluated 24 hours after a helmet-to-helmet collision during a football game. He had no loss of consciousness but developed headache, dizziness, and difficulty concentrating. Neurologic examination is normal, and head CT performed in the emergency department showed no acute abnormality. His symptoms are improving but persist with reading. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Allow return to full-contact practice today
B: Begin a gradual return-to-learn and return-to-play protocol after brief relative rest
C: Keep him out of school and sports until he is completely symptom-free at rest
D: Obtain a repeat head CT before resuming school activities
E: Start prophylactic anticonvulsant therapy before return to sports

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with 24 hours of crampy abdominal pain, progressive abdominal distension, nausea, and bilious vomiting. He has not passed flatus or stool since symptom onset. Medical history is significant for an open sigmoid colectomy 8 years ago. Temperature is 37.8°C (100.0°F), blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, pulse is 96/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The abdomen is distended and tympanitic with diffuse mild tenderness but no rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 11,200/mm3 and serum lactate of 1.4 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
A: Immediate exploratory laparotomy
B: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
C: Colonoscopy to identify an obstructing colonic lesion
D: Small-bowel follow-through with oral barium contrast

stem: A 68-year-old man with a 3-month history of prostate cancer presents with 2 days of worsening mid-thoracic back pain and progressive difficulty walking. He now has bilateral leg weakness, numbness below the umbilicus, and urinary hesitancy. Examination shows spastic paraparesis, hyperreflexia in both legs, and a sensory level at T10. He is afebrile and has no history of trauma. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Administer intravenous dexamethasone and obtain urgent MRI of the spine
B: Perform lumbar puncture to evaluate for leptomeningeal carcinomatosis
C: Obtain plain radiographs of the thoracic spine and begin physical therapy
D: Administer intravenous antibiotics and obtain blood cultures
E: Schedule elective surgical decompression after outpatient oncology evaluation

stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 6-month history of progressive muscle weakness and wasting. He reports difficulty buttoning his shirt and frequent tripping due to foot drop. Physical examination reveals fasciculations in the tongue and bilateral hand intrinsics. Deep tendon reflexes are hyperactive in the lower extremities, and the Babinski sign is positive bilaterally. Sensory examination is intact. Electromyography shows widespread denervation with fibrillation potentials and large motor unit potentials. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
D: Myasthenia gravis

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother due to a 2-day history of sore throat, fever, and difficulty swallowing. On examination, his temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), his pharynx is erythematous with exudate, and his anterior cervical lymph nodes are tender and enlarged. A rapid streptococcal antigen test is positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Initiate oral penicillin VK for 10 days.
B: Prescribe azithromycin for 5 days due to penicillin allergy.
C: Order a throat culture and withhold antibiotics until results are available.
D: Administer intramuscular benzathine penicillin G once.
E: Recommend supportive care only and monitor for complications.

stem: A 74-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after falling down the stairs. He has a history of nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily. On examination, he is confused with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8. A noncontrast CT scan of the head reveals a large right-sided subdural hematoma with midline shift. His blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, heart rate is 90/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Laboratory studies show an international normalized ratio of 1.1 and a partial thromboplastin time of 32 seconds. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Administer four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
D: Administer vitamin K intravenously

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of right-sided facial droop and inability to fully close her right eye. She also reports decreased tearing on the right side and mild discomfort behind her right ear. On examination, she has weakness of the right forehead, orbicularis oculi, and orbicularis oris muscles. The remainder of the neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Oral glucocorticoids alone
B: Oral glucocorticoids plus an antiviral agent
C: Surgical decompression of the facial nerve
D: Supportive care with eye protection only

stem: A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is admitted to the hospital for management of a diabetic foot ulcer. His current regimen includes metformin and glipizide, but his blood glucose levels remain elevated. The physician decides to start insulin therapy. Which of the following insulin regimens is most appropriate for this patient?
A: Basal insulin glargine at bedtime and prandial insulin aspart with meals
D: Insulin detemir twice daily

stem: A 28-year-old woman, G1P0, at 28 weeks gestation comes to the clinic after a minor motor vehicle collision. She is hemodynamically stable and has mild abdominal bruising. Blood type is O Rh-negative, and the antibody screen is negative. Fetal heart tracing is reassuring. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to prevent Rh alloimmunization?
A: Administer anti-D immune globulin now
B: Delay anti-D immune globulin until 34 weeks gestation
C: Withhold anti-D immune globulin unless the fetus is Rh-positive
D: Administer anti-D immune globulin only if she develops vaginal bleeding
E: Obtain a Kleihauer-Betke test and withhold anti-D immune globulin if negative

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 12 hours of crampy abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. He has a history of an appendectomy 5 years ago. Physical examination reveals a distended, tympanic abdomen with high-pitched bowel sounds. An upright abdominal radiograph shows multiple air-fluid levels and dilated loops of small bowel. After initial resuscitation with intravenous fluids and nasogastric decompression, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Emergent exploratory laparotomy
B: Abdominal computed tomography with intravenous contrast
C: Upper gastrointestinal series with small bowel follow-through
D: Diagnostic laparoscopy
E: Observation with serial abdominal examinations for 48 hours without imaging

stem: A 32-year-old woman, G3P2, at 34 weeks' gestation presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of painless, bright red vaginal bleeding that started 1 hour ago. She reports no contractions, abdominal pain, or trauma. Her prenatal course has been unremarkable, and she has not had a third-trimester ultrasound. On examination, vital signs are stable, the uterus is soft and nontender, and the fetal heart rate tracing is reassuring with a baseline of 140/min and normal variability. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Perform a digital cervical examination to assess dilation
C: Obtain a transabdominal ultrasound to assess placental location
D: Proceed immediately to emergency cesarean delivery
E: Perform an amniocentesis to assess fetal lung maturity

stem: A 56-year-old woman comes to the office because of vaginal dryness and pain during intercourse for 8 months. Her last menstrual period was 4 years ago. She has no hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal bleeding, or vaginal discharge. Regular use of vaginal moisturizers and lubricants for 3 months has provided inadequate relief. Her uterus is intact. Pelvic examination shows pale, thin vaginal mucosa with loss of rugae. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
A: Low-dose vaginal estradiol alone
D: Transdermal estradiol alone

stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after suddenly developing inability to move both legs while at work. Earlier that day, she learned that her older brother had died in a motor vehicle accident. She has no history of neurologic disease. On examination, she reports complete paralysis of both legs, but muscle tone, deep tendon reflexes, and sensation are normal; she withdraws both legs briskly from painful stimulation. When distracted, she briefly moves her legs spontaneously. MRI of the brain and spinal cord and laboratory studies are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A: Conversion disorder (functional neurologic symptom disorder)
D: Multiple sclerosis

stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of congestive heart failure (ejection fraction 30%) presents with confusion and fatigue over the past week. He has gained 3 kg in the last month. His medications include metoprolol, lisinopril, furosemide, and aspirin. Serum sodium is 122 mEq/L. Which is the most likely cause of his hyponatremia?
A: Congestive heart failure with volume overload
D: SIADH from lung cancer

stem: A 4-month-old girl is brought to the clinic for a follow-up visit. Three days ago, she was evaluated in the emergency department for a temperature of 39.4°C (103°F) and irritability. Urinalysis and urine culture obtained via catheterization showed pyuria and grew >50,000 colony-forming units/mL of Escherichia coli. She was started on oral cefdinir. Today, she is afebrile and feeding well. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis
D: Renal and bladder ultrasonography

stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her roommate because of sudden inability to move her left arm and leg that began 3 hours ago. She reports no headache, vision changes, or numbness. Earlier that day, she learned that her fiancé had ended their engagement. She has no significant medical history and takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. She appears calm and unconcerned about her symptoms. On examination, she is unable to lift her left leg off the bed. When asked to lift her right leg against resistance, the examiner feels downward pressure from the left heel. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric, and plantar responses are flexor bilaterally. Sensation is intact. Noncontrast CT scan of the head shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Obtain MRI of the brain and cervical spine
C: Explain the diagnosis to the patient and refer for physical therapy and psychotherapy
D: Confront the patient with evidence that her symptoms are feigned

stem: A 58-year-old man with hypertension and a 35-pack-year smoking history presents for routine follow-up. He has no history of diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg, and body mass index is 29 kg/m². Fasting laboratory studies show total cholesterol of 242 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol of 168 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol of 41 mg/dL, and triglycerides of 165 mg/dL. He takes amlodipine and has no contraindications to statin therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Initiate a moderate-intensity statin
D: Recommend lifestyle modification alone
E: Repeat the lipid panel in 6 months

stem: A 62-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer treated 4 years ago comes to the emergency department because of worsening midback pain for 3 weeks and difficulty walking for 2 days. The pain awakens her at night and worsens when she coughs. This morning, she was unable to urinate despite feeling that her bladder was full. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F). Examination shows tenderness over the lower thoracic spine, bilateral hip flexion strength of 3/5, increased patellar reflexes, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Pinprick sensation is diminished below the umbilicus. Bladder ultrasonography shows 650 mL of retained urine. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic study?
A: Noncontrast CT of the head
B: Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid analysis
C: Urgent MRI of the entire spine with and without contrast
D: Radionuclide bone scan

stem: A 24-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 1, comes to the office for a routine health maintenance examination. She is sexually active with one male partner and uses condoms inconsistently. She has no chronic medical conditions and takes no medications. Her last Pap test was performed 12 months ago and was reported as atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US); reflex HPV testing was negative. She asks what cervical cancer screening she needs today. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in cervical cancer screening?
A: No cervical cancer screening is indicated at this time
D: Cervical cytology and high-risk HPV cotesting

stem: A 55-year-old man undergoes a routine colonoscopy, which reveals a 1.5 cm pedunculated polyp in the sigmoid colon. Histopathological examination of the polypectomy specimen shows a tubular adenoma with high-grade dysplasia. Which of the following molecular alterations is most likely to be associated with the development of this lesion?
A: APC gene mutation
D: BRAF mutation

stem: A 64-year-old man is hospitalized for Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis and receives intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin based on susceptibility testing. Ten days after treatment begins, his serum creatinine concentration has increased from 0.9 mg/dL to 2.4 mg/dL. His fever has resolved, blood cultures are now negative, and his blood pressure has remained normal throughout hospitalization. Urine output is 1.8 L/day. Examination shows no rash, edema, or signs of volume depletion. Urinalysis shows granular casts without hematuria or pyuria. Renal ultrasonography shows no hydronephrosis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's acute kidney injury?
A: Immune-mediated inflammation of the renal interstitium
B: Direct injury to proximal tubular epithelial cells
C: Deposition of circulating immune complexes in glomeruli
D: Reduced renal perfusion causing increased tubular sodium reabsorption

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use presents with fatigue, arthralgias, and right upper quadrant discomfort. Laboratory studies show elevated serum aminotransferases and positive anti-HCV antibodies. A liver biopsy is performed. Histologic examination reveals dense portal lymphoid aggregates with germinal center formation, bile duct epithelial injury, and mild interface hepatitis. There is also prominent macrovesicular steatosis involving approximately 40% of hepatocytes. Which of the following histologic findings is most characteristic of this patient's underlying liver disease?
A: Lymphocytic infiltrate within portal tracts with bile duct damage and steatosis
B: Ground-glass hepatocytes with positive orcein staining
C: Mallory-Denk bodies with neutrophilic infiltration and pericellular fibrosis
D: Florid duct lesions with granulomatous destruction of bile ducts
E: Piecemeal necrosis with plasma cell predominance and rosette formation

stem: A 68-year-old man presents for an annual physical examination. Digital rectal examination reveals a firm, irregular prostate with a palpable nodule. Serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is 12 ng/mL. A transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy is performed, and the pathology report shows a Gleason score of 4 + 3 = 7. Which of the following best describes the Gleason grading pattern of this tumor?
A: Predominantly well-formed glandular structures with some poorly formed glands (Gleason pattern 3) and some fused or poorly defined glandular structures (Gleason pattern 4).
B: Predominantly poorly formed glands (Gleason pattern 4) with some well-formed glands (Gleason pattern 3).
C: Uniform small, closely packed glands (Gleason pattern 1) and irregular infiltrative glands (Gleason pattern 2).
D: Cribriform or comedonecrosis patterns (Gleason pattern 5) with some well-formed glands (Gleason pattern 3).
E: Single infiltrative cells or sheets of cells (Gleason pattern 5) with some fused glands (Gleason pattern 4).

stem: A 48-year-old woman comes to the clinic due to a painless lump in her neck that she noticed 3 weeks ago. She reports mild heat intolerance and occasional palpitations over the past month. Physical examination reveals a nontender, mobile, 2-cm nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid gland with no cervical lymphadenopathy. Thyroid ultrasonography confirms a 2.1-cm solitary, solid nodule in the right lobe. Laboratory evaluation shows a serum TSH level of 0.15 µU/mL (reference: 0.4–4.0 µU/mL) and a free thyroxine (T4) level of 1.6 ng/dL (reference: 0.8–1.8 ng/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Core-needle biopsy
D: Serum thyroglobulin measurement

stem: A 6-week-old infant is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever and irritability. The infant's temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), and the physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory results show a white blood cell count of 12,000 cells/μL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Obtain a complete sepsis workup, including blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid cultures
B: Administer antipyretics and discharge home with close follow-up
C: Prescribe oral antibiotics and schedule a follow-up visit in 48 hours
D: Perform a chest radiograph to rule out pneumonia
E: Order a urinalysis and culture, but defer lumbar puncture

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of lower abdominal pain and vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. She has a history of pelvic inflammatory disease. On examination, her blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, heart rate is 90/min, and abdomen is tender in the left lower quadrant without rebound. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a gestational sac in the left adnexa with no intrauterine pregnancy. Serum beta-hCG is 1500 mIU/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A: Ectopic pregnancy
D: Threatened abortion

stem: A 48-year-old woman who works as a data entry clerk reports a 6-month history of numbness and tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers of her right hand that worsens at night and often wakes her from sleep. She reports that shaking her hand provides temporary relief. Physical examination reveals decreased sensation over the palmar surface of the affected fingers and a positive response to tapping over the volar wrist. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's symptoms?
A: Compression of the median nerve at the wrist
B: Compression of the radial nerve at the elbow
C: Compression of the ulnar nerve at the elbow
D: Cervical nerve root compression at C6-C7

stem: A 6-week-old male infant presents with a 2-day history of fever (38.8°C), irritability, and poor feeding. He has no vomiting, diarrhea, or respiratory symptoms. Urinalysis shows positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites, and the urine Gram stain reveals gram-negative rods. A renal ultrasound is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Begin empiric intravenous antibiotics and obtain a voiding cystourethrogram
B: Begin empiric oral antibiotics and schedule a follow-up in 48 hours
C: Obtain a blood culture and begin empiric intravenous antibiotics
D: Obtain a renal scan and begin empiric oral antibiotics
E: Repeat urinalysis in 24 hours before initiating antibiotics

stem: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of periumbilical pain that migrated to the right lower quadrant, accompanied by anorexia and nausea. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), heart rate is 100 bpm, and blood pressure is 120/78 mm Hg. Abdominal examination reveals tenderness and voluntary guarding at McBurney point. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 14,500/mm³. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
A: Abdominal CT scan with intravenous contrast
D: Graded compression ultrasonography

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician complaining of numbness and tingling in her right hand that has been worsening over the past 6 months. She describes the symptoms as primarily affecting her thumb, index finger, middle finger, and the radial half of her ring finger. She notes that the sensations are worse at night and often wake her up, prompting her to shake her hand for relief. She works as a data entry clerk and spends long hours typing. Physical examination reveals decreased light touch sensation in the median nerve distribution. Tapping over the volar aspect of the wrist at the flexor retinaculum reproduces her paresthesias. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
A: MRI of the cervical spine
D: Ulnar nerve conduction studies

stem: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, presents for her 6-week postpartum visit. She delivered a healthy baby at term without complications. She reports feeling sad, exhausted, and overwhelmed most days since delivery. She has difficulty falling asleep even when the baby sleeps, has poor appetite, and often feels guilty that she is not a good mother. She denies suicidal ideation. She has no prior psychiatric history, and her physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Begin cognitive behavioral therapy and screen for bipolar disorder before starting medication
B: Reassure her that these symptoms are normal postpartum blues and will resolve spontaneously
C: Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and schedule follow-up in 6 months
D: Admit her to the hospital for inpatient psychiatric treatment
E: Obtain thyroid-stimulating hormone and free T4 only, and defer psychiatric treatment until results return

stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motorcycle collision. He is agitated and combative. His blood pressure is 88/56 mmHg, pulse is 128/min, and respirations are 32/min with gurgling sounds. There is blood in the oropharynx and a laceration over the right thigh with pulsatile bleeding that is being controlled with direct pressure by paramedics. Oxygen saturation cannot be obtained due to poor waveform. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Apply a pelvic binder
B: Obtain intravenous access and begin fluid resuscitation
D: Perform a focused assessment with sonography for trauma
E: Suction the oropharynx and assess the airway

stem: A 52-year-old woman comes to the office because of hot flashes, night sweats, and irregular menses for the past 6 months. She has no significant medical history, takes no medications, and has a body mass index of 25 kg/m². Her last menstrual period was 2 months ago. She requests treatment for her symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
A: Prescribe combined estrogen-progestin therapy
D: Start gabapentin for symptom relief

stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to sudden-onset, severe right lower quadrant abdominal pain that began 2 hours ago while she was exercising. She has had two episodes of vomiting since the pain started. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago, and her menses are regular. She has no history of sexually transmitted infections. Vital signs are temperature 37.1°C (98.8°F), blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, and pulse 105/min. Physical examination shows right lower quadrant tenderness with voluntary guarding. Pelvic examination reveals a tender fullness in the right adnexa. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
A: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis
C: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis
D: Pelvic ultrasonography

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with absence of menses for 7 months. Her menstrual cycles were previously regular. Eight months ago, she underwent suction curettage for an incomplete spontaneous abortion. She takes no medications and reports no weight changes, excessive exercise, headaches, or nipple discharge. BMI is 23 kg/m². Pelvic examination is normal. Serum β-hCG is negative, and serum TSH, prolactin, and FSH concentrations are within reference ranges. She has no withdrawal bleeding after a progestin challenge or after a subsequent course of estrogen followed by progestin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A: Asherman syndrome
D: Primary ovarian insufficiency

stem: A 62-year-old man is evaluated for 3 months of intermittent rectal bleeding and a 4-kg weight loss. Colonoscopy reveals a 4-cm ulcerated mass in the sigmoid colon; biopsy shows moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. The remainder of the colon is normal. Physical examination shows no abdominal masses, hepatomegaly, or lymphadenopathy. Hemoglobin concentration is 10.8 g/dL, and liver enzyme activities are within normal limits. Carcinoembryonic antigen level is 6.2 ng/mL. He is scheduled for sigmoid colectomy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?"
A: CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast
B: Endoscopic ultrasonography of the sigmoid lesion
C: Fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan of the whole body
D: MRI of the pelvis with contrast

stem: A 48-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol use presents with 18 hours of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and repeated vomiting. Serum lipase is markedly elevated. Contrast-enhanced CT shows acute interstitial edematous pancreatitis without necrosis or fluid collections. He is tachycardic, has dry mucous membranes, and his blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. After initial analgesia and antiemetics, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Begin aggressive intravenous lactated Ringer solution and monitor urine output and hemodynamic status
D: Keep the patient without oral intake until the serum lipase normalizes

stem: A previously healthy 8-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of fever and irritability. Her temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F). She appears well hydrated, and physical examination shows no source of infection. A catheterized urine specimen has 50 white blood cells per high-power field and is positive for nitrites. Urine culture grows greater than 100,000 colony-forming units per milliliter of Escherichia coli. She is treated with a 10-day course of oral cephalexin and becomes afebrile within 48 hours. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Computed tomography of the kidneys
D: Technetium-99m dimercaptosuccinic acid scintigraphy

stem: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 1, presents for a routine well-woman examination. Her last cervical cancer screening was 4 years ago and was reported as normal. She has no new symptoms. Medical history is unremarkable, and she takes no medications. She has been in a monogamous relationship for 5 years. Physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Human papillomavirus testing
D: Repeat cytology in 5 years
E: Screen with cytology and human papillomavirus testing

stem: A 79-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her son due to acute confusion and visual hallucinations that began 2 days ago. Her son notes that she has experienced mild, gradual memory loss over the past 2 years but remained independent in all activities of daily living until this week. Over the past 48 hours, her mental status has fluctuated significantly; she is drowsy during the day but becomes agitated and fearful at night, claiming there are strangers in her room. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 96/min. On examination, she is inattentive, unable to count backward from 20, and repeatedly drifts off to sleep during the interview. Urinalysis is positive for leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and numerous bacteria. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A: Alzheimer disease
D: Frontotemporal dementia

stem: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, comes to the emergency department because of 1 day of vaginal spotting and mild left lower quadrant pain. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. She has no history of pelvic inflammatory disease or tubal surgery. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows mild left lower quadrant tenderness without rebound or guarding. Pelvic examination shows a closed cervix with scant blood in the vault and no adnexal mass. Serum β-hCG concentration is 1,200 mIU/mL. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows an empty uterus with an endometrial thickness of 9 mm, no adnexal mass, and no free fluid in the pelvis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Diagnostic laparoscopy
D: Repeat serum β-hCG measurement in 48 hours

stem: A 9-year-old girl with sickle cell disease is brought to the emergency department because of 2 days of fever and increasing pallor. She has had mild cough and rhinorrhea. Her temperature is 39.2 C (102.6 F), pulse is 132/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. She appears pale and tired. The spleen is palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 4.8 g/dL, leukocyte count 11,000/mm3, platelet count 410,000/mm3, and reticulocyte count 0.3%. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A: Acute chest syndrome
D: Hepatic sequestration crisis

stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the physician 3 days after sustaining a head injury during a football game. He was struck helmet-to-helmet and briefly felt dazed but did not lose consciousness. He sat out the rest of the game as required by his coach. Since then he has had mild headache and difficulty concentrating on schoolwork, both of which are improving. He has no vomiting, focal weakness, or worsening symptoms. Neurologic examination, including cognitive testing and balance assessment, is normal. He is eager to return to football practice this week. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding his return to sports?
A: Begin a graduated, stepwise return-to-play protocol now that he is asymptomatic at rest
B: Clear him for full-contact practice immediately because his examination is normal
C: Obtain an MRI of the brain before allowing any return to physical activity
D: Restrict him from all physical activity, including light exercise, for one month
E: Withhold return to play until he passes a formal neuropsychological test battery

stem: A 45-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after receiving the second unit of packed red blood cells for treatment of iron-deficiency anemia. She reports sudden onset of fever, chills, and lower back pain. Physical examination reveals a temperature of 38.9°C (102°F), blood pressure of 110/70 mm Hg, and tachycardia. The transfusion is immediately stopped. Laboratory evaluation shows a positive direct antiglobulin test (Coombs test) and evidence of intravascular hemolysis, including hemoglobinuria and decreased haptoglobin levels. The blood bank confirms that the patient received blood that was ABO-compatible but carried a minor antigen mismatch against a naturally occurring antibody. Which of the following is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism responsible for this patient's reaction?
A: Antibody-mediated complement activation leading to intravascular hemolysis
B: Antibody-mediated phagocytosis by macrophages in the spleen
C: Cytokine release from donor leukocytes causing systemic inflammation
D: Donor antibodies reacting against recipient HLA class I antigens
E: Donor plasma antibodies reacting against recipient red blood cell antigens

stem: A 19-year-old college soccer player is evaluated 2 days after sustaining a head-to-head collision. She was briefly dazed but did not lose consciousness. She has headache, light sensitivity, and difficulty concentrating, but neurologic examination is normal. She has been resting in a dark room and avoiding schoolwork. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Begin a gradual return to regular cognitive and physical activity as tolerated
B: Obtain magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before resuming activity
C: Prescribe strict physical and cognitive rest until all symptoms resolve
D: Recommend return to competitive play after 24 hours without symptoms
E: Start prophylactic amitriptyline for posttraumatic headache

stem: A 64-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia develops substernal chest pressure while climbing stairs. The pain persists at rest and is associated with diaphoresis and nausea. In the emergency department, temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure is 148/86 mm Hg, and pulse is 96/min. Examination shows no heart failure. Electrocardiography demonstrates 2-mm ST-segment elevations in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST-segment depressions in leads I and aVL. He has no history of bleeding, recent surgery, or stroke. Aspirin was administered on arrival. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Administer intravenous unfractionated heparin and arrange immediate coronary angiography with percutaneous coronary intervention
B: Administer intravenous alteplase and reassess the electrocardiogram in 24 hours
C: Begin a high-intensity statin and schedule an outpatient exercise stress test
D: Administer intravenous nitroglycerin and observe for resolution of symptoms
E: Administer oral warfarin and admit for telemetry monitoring

stem: A 55-year-old woman comes to the office because of recurrent episodes of vertigo over the past 2 weeks. She describes the sensation as a spinning sensation lasting several seconds, triggered by turning her head to the right. Episodes are associated with mild nausea but no hearing loss or tinnitus. She has no history of trauma or ear infection. On examination, she has no spontaneous nystagmus, and her auditory and neurological exams are normal. Dix-Hallpike maneuver is performed and shows delayed onset of transient right-beating nystagmus with the head turned to the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
D: Multiple sclerosis

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with a history of difficulty concentrating at work, frequent procrastination, and chronic forgetfulness since childhood. He reports feeling restless and often interrupts colleagues during meetings. He has no history of manic or hypomanic episodes, and his mood is euthymic. A trial of sertraline for presumed anxiety was ineffective. Vital signs and physical examination are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Administer the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale
C: Order a sleep study to evaluate for sleep apnea
D: Refer for neuropsychological testing

stem: A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife due to a 1-day history of fever, severe headache, and confusion. His temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), blood pressure is 140/85 mm Hg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 18/min. Physical examination reveals nuchal rigidity. Neurologic examination shows a right-sided pronator drift and a hyperactive deep tendon reflex in the right upper extremity. Blood cultures are obtained. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Administer ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and dexamethasone
C: Obtain a noncontrast CT scan of the head
D: Obtain an MRI scan of the brain

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and fatigue for the past two months. Physical examination reveals multiple firm, nontender lymph nodes in the neck and axillae. Excisional lymph node biopsy shows a diffuse infiltrate of large lymphoid cells with prominent nucleoli and high mitotic activity, effacing the normal nodal architecture. Immunohistochemistry demonstrates that the neoplastic cells are positive for CD20 and negative for CD3. A translocation involving MYC is not detected.
A: Burkitt lymphoma
D: Mantle cell lymphoma

stem: A 55-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of severe, sharp, shooting pain on the right side of her face that has been occurring for the past month. She states that the pain lasts for only a few seconds but is excruciating. The episodes are frequently triggered by brushing her teeth, chewing, or feeling a cold breeze against her face. She has no history of headaches, vision changes, or jaw claudication. Vital signs are within normal limits. Neurological examination reveals normal facial sensation, symmetric facial muscle strength, and normal corneal reflexes. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy for this patient's condition?
A: Amitriptyline
D: Prednisone

stem: A 67-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for a routine health maintenance visit. He has no complaints and has never had this type of visit before. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history but quit 5 years ago. His medical history includes hypertension and hyperlipidemia, both controlled with medication. He has no family history of aortic aneurysm. Vital signs are within normal limits, and abdominal examination reveals no pulsatile mass or bruits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Reassure the patient that no further workup is needed
B: Order a CT angiogram of the abdomen and pelvis
C: Order a one-time abdominal ultrasound to screen for abdominal aortic aneurysm
D: Refer to vascular surgery for evaluation
E: Repeat abdominal examination annually to monitor for a pulsatile mass

stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of chronic hepatitis C undergoes a liver biopsy, which shows extensive scarring with nodule formation and prominent bile duct proliferation. Which histological feature is most likely to be present in this patient's liver biopsy specimen?
A: Regenerative nodules
D: Steatosis

stem: A 42-year-old woman is hospitalized with 12 hours of severe epigastric pain radiating to her back, nausea, and vomiting. She does not drink alcohol and takes no medications. On admission, her serum lipase is 1,860 U/L (normal: 10–60), alanine aminotransferase is 210 U/L, and total bilirubin is 1.1 mg/dL. Right upper quadrant ultrasonography shows multiple gallstones without gallbladder wall thickening; the common bile duct measures 4 mm. She receives intravenous lactated Ringer solution and analgesia. She has no hypotension, hypoxemia, or acute kidney injury during hospitalization. After 48 hours, her pain has resolved, her liver tests are improving, and she tolerates a regular diet. Which of the following is the most appropriate management to prevent recurrence?
A: Schedule laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 6 weeks
B: Perform laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the current hospitalization
C: Perform endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with sphincterotomy instead of cholecystectomy
D: Begin long-term ursodeoxycholic acid therapy
E: Recommend a low-fat diet and reserve cholecystectomy for recurrent symptoms

stem: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 9 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of persistent nausea and vomiting for the past 2 weeks. She has been unable to tolerate solid food or liquids for the past 3 days and reports dizziness on standing. She has lost 4 kg (9 lb) since her last prenatal visit 3 weeks ago. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 112/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Examination shows dry mucous membranes and decreased skin turgor. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Urinalysis shows 3+ ketones and a specific gravity of 1.030. Serum studies show a potassium concentration of 3.0 mEq/L and a chloride concentration of 92 mEq/L. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a single intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity consistent with 9 weeks' gestation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Administration of oral pyridoxine and doxylamine
B: Administration of oral ginger supplements and dietary modification
C: Intravenous administration of 5% dextrose in normal saline with potassium and thiamine
D: Intravenous administration of methylprednisolone
E: Placement of a nasogastric tube for enteral feeding

stem: A 68-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with a 6-month history of cramping pain in both calves that occurs after walking two blocks and resolves with rest. He has no pain at rest and no tissue loss. Physical examination shows diminished dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally. Ankle-brachial index is 0.65 bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
A: Aspirin therapy and a supervised walking program
D: Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty

stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for 3 weeks of increasing thirst, frequent urination, nocturnal enuresis, fatigue, and a 4-kg (9-lb) weight loss. He has no fever, vomiting, or abdominal pain. His mother has autoimmune thyroid disease. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg, pulse is 92/min, and respirations are 18/min. Physical examination shows mild dehydration without Kussmaul respirations or altered mental status. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
A: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing absolute insulin deficiency
B: Decreased responsiveness of peripheral tissues to insulin due to obesity-related insulin resistance
C: Excessive secretion of antidiuretic hormone causing dilutional hyponatremia
D: Increased cortisol production causing hyperglycemia and muscle wasting
E: Renal tubular resistance to antidiuretic hormone causing inability to concentrate urine

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 37 weeks gestation presents for a routine prenatal visit. She reports no symptoms of urinary tract infection. A urine culture performed at 16 weeks was negative. Group B Streptococcus (GBS) screening at 35 weeks was positive. Her medical history is significant only for well-controlled gestational diabetes. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
A: Administer intrapartum penicillin G 5 million units IV, followed by 2.5 million units IV every 4 hours until delivery.
B: Administer intrapartum penicillin G 5 million units IM, followed by 2.5 million units IM every 4 hours until delivery.
C: Administer intrapartum penicillin G 2.5 million units IV every 4 hours until delivery without a loading dose.
D: Obtain a repeat urine culture and administer intrapartum prophylaxis only if culture is positive.
E: Obtain a repeat GBS vaginal-rectal culture and administer intrapartum prophylaxis only if culture is positive.

stem: A 4-month-old girl comes to the clinic for a well-child visit. She was born at term and has had no significant illnesses. Her immunization records show she received the first doses of DTaP, inactivated poliovirus vaccine, Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, and rotavirus vaccine at 2 months of age. She is now due for her 4-month vaccines. Her mother reports that the child has been healthy with no fevers, vomiting, or diarrhea. On examination, the infant is afebrile and appears well. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Administer the second doses of DTaP, inactivated poliovirus vaccine, Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, and rotavirus vaccine
B: Delay all vaccines until 6 months of age to reduce injection burden
C: Give only the second dose of DTaP and postpone the remaining vaccines
D: Measure serum antibody titers before giving additional vaccines
E: Substitute live attenuated vaccines for the scheduled inactivated vaccines

stem: A 29-year-old woman, G1P0, at 33 weeks' gestation presents to the obstetric triage unit with a headache and blurry vision for the past several hours. She has had no prenatal care since 20 weeks due to lack of insurance. Blood pressure is 168/112 mm Hg on two readings taken 15 minutes apart. She reports epigastric pain but denies vaginal bleeding or leakage of fluid. Fetal heart rate tracing is reassuring with a baseline of 140/min and moderate variability. Laboratory studies show platelet count of 90,000/mm3, AST 110 U/L, ALT 98 U/L, and serum creatinine 1.3 mg/dL. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 0.4. Magnesium sulfate infusion is started for seizure prophylaxis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Administer betamethasone and manage expectantly until 34 weeks
B: Start oral labetalol and discharge home with strict blood pressure monitoring
C: Proceed with delivery after administering an antihypertensive to control severe range blood pressure
D: Perform an urgent cesarean delivery regardless of blood pressure control
E: Obtain a 24-hour urine protein collection before deciding on delivery timing

stem: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of a dry cough for 4 weeks. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Lisinopril was started 6 weeks ago. His blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate replacement for lisinopril?
A: Amlodipine
D: Metoprolol

stem: A 65-year-old woman who underwent elective hip replacement surgery 5 days ago develops sudden onset of dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Her platelet count, which was normal preoperatively, is now 48,000/µL. A CT pulmonary angiogram confirms bilateral pulmonary emboli. She has no prior history of heparin exposure. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
A: Discontinue all heparin and initiate argatroban
C: Start fondaparinux and continue low-molecular-weight heparin
D: Perform platelet transfusion and start warfarin
E: Increase the dose of unfractionated heparin

stem: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of fatigue, dizziness, and cold intolerance for 2 weeks. Over the past 8 months, she has restricted her food intake to fewer than 500 kcal/day and runs 10 km daily; she believes she is overweight despite reassurance from others. Her last menstrual period was 5 months ago. She is 165 cm tall and weighs 40 kg (BMI 14.7 kg/m2). Her temperature is 35.6°C (96.1°F), pulse is 38/min, and blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg supine with a drop to 65/40 mm Hg on standing. Physical examination shows dry skin, fine hair over the arms and back, and cool extremities. Serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L and serum phosphorus is 2.0 mg/dL. ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a QTc of 490 ms. She insists she feels fine and asks to go home to prepare for a school exam. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Admit to the hospital for medical stabilization and monitored nutritional rehabilitation
B: Begin outpatient family-based therapy with weekly weight checks
C: Discharge home with a prescription for olanzapine to promote weight gain
D: Prescribe fluoxetine and schedule cognitive behavioral therapy as an outpatient
E: Start estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive therapy to restore menses and protect bone density

stem: A 68-year-old woman is hospitalized with nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, and crampy abdominal pain. She has not passed flatus for 24 hours. She underwent hysterectomy 10 years ago. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, pulse is 92/min, and respirations are 18/min. The abdomen is distended and tympanitic with mild diffuse tenderness but no guarding or rebound tenderness. CT scan of the abdomen shows dilated proximal small-bowel loops with a transition point in the distal ileum and no free air, bowel-wall hypoenhancement, or mesenteric edema. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Administer broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
B: Begin nonoperative management with nasogastric decompression and intravenous fluids
D: Proceed with emergent exploratory laparotomy

stem: A 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to severe right-sided head pain. The pain started abruptly 30 minutes ago and is localized behind his right eye. He rates the pain as a 10/10 and describes it as "stabbing." He has had similar episodes every night for the past week, usually waking him from sleep. During the interview, the patient is pacing around the exam room and appears deeply agitated. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows right conjunctival injection, lacrimation, and mild right-sided ptosis. Neurologic examination is otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient's current symptoms?
A: 100% oxygen via nonrebreather mask
D: Intravenous metoclopramide

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 12 hours of periumbilical pain that has migrated to the right lower quadrant. She reports nausea and anorexia. On examination, she has tenderness at McBurney’s point with rebound and guarding. Temperature is 38.5°C, and white blood cell count is 14,000/mm³ with 85% neutrophils. Urinalysis is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
A: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
D: Plain abdominal radiography

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the office due to recurrent episodes of intense fear that have occurred over the past 3 months. She describes these episodes as coming on suddenly and peaking within minutes, accompanied by palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, chest pain, nausea, and a fear of losing control or 'going crazy.' Between episodes, she is anxious about having another attack and has begun avoiding public transportation and large crowds. She has no history of substance use or medical conditions. A physical examination and electrocardiogram are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A: Generalized anxiety disorder
D: Specific phobia

stem: A 28-year-old woman has chronic diarrhea, bloating, fatigue, and a 6-kg weight loss over 4 months. Laboratory studies show iron-deficiency anemia and positive IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies. Duodenal biopsy is performed. Which histologic finding is most likely?
A: Villous blunting with crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes
B: Foveolar hyperplasia with elongated gastric pits and expanded lamina propria
D: Aplasia of colonic crypts with abundant apoptotic debris
E: Diffuse mucosal infiltration by signet-ring cells

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue. She has iron-deficiency anemia and a family history of autoimmune disease. Upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsy is performed. Histologic examination of the biopsy specimen reveals villous blunting, crypt hyperplasia, and an increased number of intraepithelial lymphocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A: Autoimmune enteropathy
D: Giardiasis

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue. Laboratory findings show iron-deficiency anemia and elevated tissue transglutaminase IgA antibodies. An upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsy is performed. Histologic examination of the biopsy specimen reveals increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, crypt hyperplasia, and partial villous atrophy. Which of the following histologic features is most characteristic of this patient's condition?
A: Subepithelial collagen deposition
C: Neutrophilic infiltration of crypts with crypt abscesses
D: Flattening of villi with a dense lymphocytic infiltrate in the lamina propria
E: Eosinophilic infiltration of the mucosa and submucosa

stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the clinic 2 days after sustaining a head collision during a soccer match. He did not lose consciousness but developed an immediate headache, mild dizziness, and difficulty concentrating. He was removed from the game immediately and has rested at home since. His headache has improved to mild intensity, and his dizziness has resolved, but he reports mild fatigue when reading. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination shows a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15, and the neurologic examination, including cranial nerves, coordination, and gait, is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Complete physical and cognitive rest until all symptoms resolve
B: Immediate clearance for non-contact athletic conditioning
C: Noncontrast CT scan of the head to evaluate for injury
D: Prophylactic oral topiramate therapy for headache control
E: Symptom-limited resumption of light daily activities

stem: A 24-day-old male infant is brought to the emergency department for a rectal temperature of 38.3°C (100.9°F) measured at home 2 hours ago. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, has been feeding well, and appears alert and vigorous. Examination shows no focal source of infection. Laboratory studies show a normal complete blood cell count, procalcitonin, and urinalysis; blood and urine cultures are obtained. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Perform lumbar puncture and admit for empiric intravenous antibiotics
B: Discharge home with close outpatient follow-up after obtaining blood and urine cultures
C: Obtain a chest radiograph and observe without antibiotics
D: Administer oral antibiotics and reassess in 24 hours
E: Perform lumbar puncture only if the blood culture becomes positive

stem: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 30 weeks' gestation presents with regular uterine contractions every 5 minutes. She has a history of preterm labor in her previous pregnancy. Her cervix is 2 cm dilated and 50% effaced. Fetal heart rate tracing is reassuring. What is the most appropriate initial management?
A: Administer corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity and consider tocolysis
B: Start magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection and tocolysis
D: Prescribe bed rest and hydration only

stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because of a 12-hour history of fever, severe headache, and progressive confusion. She has no significant medical history and takes no medications. Her temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), pulse is 112/min, and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. She is oriented to person only. Examination shows nuchal rigidity and a right facial droop that spares the forehead. Fundoscopic examination shows bilateral papilledema. Blood cultures are obtained. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A: Acyclovir intravenously
D: MRI of the brain

stem: A 68-year-old man undergoes elective open sigmoid colectomy for diverticular disease. On postoperative day 3, he has progressive abdominal distension, nausea, and inability to tolerate oral intake. He has not passed flatus or stool since surgery.
